events.desc: Penelope Pitstop: Well, I do declare — if this isn't the most magnificently spooky entrance hall I have ever had the pleasure of walking into! Look at those portraits, just daring you to blink first. And that chandelier — oh honey, that chandelier is one strong breeze away from redecorating the floor. Now then — a guest book! In an abandoned mansion! If that isn't an invitation to start unraveling a mystery, I don't know what is.
events.thinking: There's a warmth spreading through my chest the moment I step through that door — the kind you get walking into a house that's been waiting for someone. Dust motes drifting in whatever light's getting through, and the air smells like old wood and stories nobody's told in a long time. My fingers are already tingling. Every portrait on that wall has eyes that follow you, and that chandelier looks like it's hanging on by sheer stubbornness. But what I notice first — what my body notices before my head catches up — is the people. Peter's here, and my stomach does that little flip it always does. The boys are here too, bless their hearts, all crowded together like they're already casing the place. And Uncle Sneekly — standing there in that hood like he always does, and I feel that old settling, like coming home. Dick Dastardly's lurking about with Muttley, and I should keep an eye on them, but honestly, right now everyone's here and everyone's whole and the tightness I didn't know I was carrying just... loosened. That guest book, though. A guest book in an abandoned mansion. Now who's been signing that?

events.desc: Every locked door is just a puzzle that hasn't met me yet. And somewhere in this grand old pile of dust and secrets, the Doily Diamond is waiting. I can practically feel it humming through the floorboards.

If I might direct your attention to the guest book here — a tradition of the house, you understand. Every visitor signs upon arrival. It helps me keep track of... well, of everything.
events.thinking: There's that settling in my chest — the cool stone feeling. I've just arrived. The entrance hall. Dusty, grand, full of people who don't know what I am. Good. My fingers are already mapping the room — Penelope is here, trusting, oblivious. Peter Perfect hovering nearby like a loyal dog. The Ant Hill Mob... there's a prickle at the back of my neck when I notice them watching. They see too much. Dick Dastardly — useful, impulsive, disposable. But my primary concern is Clara. She's not in this room. I need to find her, track her movements, understand where the treasure hunt will lead her. But first — I am Pemberton. The mild-mannered estate manager. I must settle into the role. The guest book on the side table... a natural thing for an estate manager to attend to. It gives me a reason to linger, to observe, to take stock of who is here and who is not. The smile comes easily. It always does.

Then we arrange.

Blimey, look at the state of this place — chandelier 'anging by a thread, dust thick enough to write your name in. *sniffs* Smells like trouble to me. Now listen — I promised Clara's old man we'd keep 'er safe, and that's exactly what we're gonna do. Nobody lets 'er out of their sight, yeah? *glances at Sneekly* And nobody — *nobody* — gets too cosy wivout us knowin' about it.

Where she can run if she needs to.

It never 'as.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly: Ah, what a MAGNIFICENT establishment! Reginald Foxworth, decorated adventurer and — as it happens — the FOREMOST authority on manor treasures in all of England. You may have heard of my exploits in the Bavarian Crypts? No? The Zanzibar Diamond Affair? Well, no matter — I shan't bore you with tales of my MANY triumphs. Now then, let me just sign the guest book here — purely as a formality, you understand. A man of my stature leaves his mark EVERYWHERE he goes.
events.thinking: There's a fizzing in my fingers already — that tightness behind my eyes that means the room is rearranging itself into levers and sequences. All these fools gathered in one dusty foyer like sheep at a gate. My chest is warm. Not from the welcome — from the count. The guest book, the coat rack, the exits to kitchen and library. Two paths, one treasure, and a room full of useful idiots. The fake medal sits heavy in my pocket like a promise. I can already feel the architecture forming — who to flatter, who to misdirect, who to send down the wrong corridor while I slip away with the prize. events.desc: Dick Dastardly: Well, well, WELL! Most illuminating, this guest book. Most illuminating INDEED. You know, in my extensive experience — the Bavarian Crypts, the Zanzibar affair, the incident in Monte Carlo which I am LEGALLY forbidden from discussing — the first clue is ALWAYS found near the hearth. The KITCHEN hearth, specifically. Old manor houses like this one always hid their valuables near the cooking fires — something about the heat protecting the parchment. It's a well-known fact among us professional treasure hunters. I suggest you ALL make haste to the kitchen immediately. Every moment you waste here is a moment the clues grow COLDER — quite literally! I shall join you presently — I simply must finish making some scholarly notes first.
events.thinking: The guest book — I've signed it, I've read it. Peter Perfect is also poking at it, the earnest fool. And he pulled Penelope aside for a private chat — probably pledging to protect her or some such nauseating chivalry. My fingers are tingling. The cool tightness is settling behind my eyes. Two exits: kitchen and library. The library has a carved stone mantelpiece with an inscription — that's where clues live. That's where treasure maps hide. The kitchen is copper pots and a stove — nothing of value to a man of my ambitions. But here's the architecture forming: if I announce loudly that the KITCHEN is where the treasure clues are, these fools will stampede toward the pots and pans while I slip quietly into the library to read that inscription. The hollow behind my navel is pulling — I need to move, to claim, to get there first. And that estate manager Sneekly — something about him makes the hair on my neck prickle. He's too smooth. Too welcoming. But no — I'll give him the benefit of the doubt. People deserve trust until they prove otherwise. Focus on the plan. Misdirect the herd, slip into the library alone.

events.desc: There is absolutely no scholarly basis for treasures being hidden near kitchen hearths. I made that up entirely. But the beautiful thing about a confident lie is that nobody checks. The LIBRARY, you see — THAT is where a proper manor keeps its secrets. Inscriptions, hidden compartments, false bookshelves — the architecture of deception! And I should know. I AM the architecture of deception.

events.desc: Peter Perfect: There we are — James Hartwell, signed and dated, proper ink. I always say, a man who doesn't sign the guest book is a man with something to hide. Now then! I couldn't help but notice that chandelier — it's listing a good fifteen degrees to starboard, which means the mounting bracket has sheared at least two of its four anchor points. I've seen this before in Victorian load-bearing ceilings — the plaster key degrades and the whole fixture becomes a pendulum waiting for an excuse. I propose — and I've thought about this carefully — that nobody stands directly beneath it until I've had a chance to inspect the ceiling joists from above. Miss Pitstop, might I suggest you stand just here, by the staircase? Structurally the soundest position in the room. I checked.
events.thinking: The guest book is under my hands now — leather, cracked, cold to the touch. My fingers find the pages and there's a small satisfaction in the gesture, the formality of it. But it's Sneekly who keeps pulling at the edge of my attention. 'Helps me keep track of everything,' he said. Everything. The way he said it — too smooth, too rehearsed. My neck prickles again. But no — Father taught me better than that. You don't accuse a man on a feeling. You watch. You prepare. And the Ant Hill Mob — good lads, they're watching Clara too. That eases something in my chest, knowing I'm not the only one standing between her and... whatever this place has in store. Now — I've signed the book, I've made my entrance. The library. Books mean maps, records, histories of the house. If there's a treasure here, the clues will be in the architecture of the place — structural, methodical. And if I can find something before anyone else, something I can bring to Clara's attention with proper gallantry... that hot weight behind my sternum pulses. Yes. The library first. But I should look at this room more carefully — that chandelier, the portraits. A thorough man examines what's in front of him before charging ahead.

James Hartwell will figure out the rest. He always does.

Penelope Pitstop: Oh, would you look at this! 'I have cities but no houses, forests but no trees, water but no fish. What am I?' Now that, ladies and gentlemen, is not just decoration — that is the first real clue in this entire mansion! And the answer, if I am not very much mistaken, is a map. A map! Which means somewhere in this library — tucked between these dusty old books, or hidden behind this very mantelpiece — there is a map waiting for us. And I would bet my grandmother's music-box key that it leads straight to the Doily Diamond!
events.thinking: Oh, my heart is hammering. The library — the smell of it hits me first, old leather and dust and something underneath, like the air itself has been holding its breath for years. The mantelpiece is right there, carved stone, and I can already see the letters from across the room. 'I have cities but no houses, forests but no trees, water but no fish. What am I?' The answer lands in my chest before my mind catches up — it's a map. A map! The prickling at my scalp is electric now, the same feeling from grandmother's attic, from the cave. Something is here. Something is waiting to be found. But I also notice — Uncle Sneekly followed me in, and Dick Dastardly too, and those two big fellows, Rock and Gravel. Peter stayed behind. The boys stayed behind. There's a tiny pull in my stomach, the awareness of who's not in the room, but it's thin — the curiosity is louder right now, much louder. The inscription is a riddle, and the answer is a map. And if there's a riddle on a mantelpiece, there's something behind that mantelpiece, or inside it, or triggered by it. My fingers are already warm. I need to interact with it.

Because if there's a room in this manor that's already been prepared as a trap... well. Why build one when someone has done the work for you? All I need to do is change the target.

Now, if you'll all excuse me — I promised to fetch lubricant for those library shelves, and I'm afraid I've been thoroughly distracted by all this excitement. I also recall that no one has checked the kitchen yet, and if there's one room in an old manor that hides its secrets well, it's the kitchen. The servants always knew more than the family, and they kept their secrets near the hearth. I shall make a quick inspection and report back. Miss Bellingham — do stay with Mr Hartwell and Clyde. This cellar is perfectly safe with them watching over things.

I mentioned it earlier — the kitchen hearth — and not a SINGLE one of you followed my advice. And now we have a missing wrench, a machine that needs three operators, and a cellar full of people arguing. A wrench is a TOOL. Where do people keep TOOLS? In a kitchen drawer, in a utility room, in a PRACTICAL space. Not in a library, not in a cellar — in a KITCHEN. I shall investigate PERSONALLY. Don't everyone rush to thank me at once.

Alone at last. And what does the kitchen offer Vincent Marsh? RAT POISON on a high shelf. A warm stove — someone has been here, or was here recently. A locked cabinet that needs a brass key. And silence. Beautiful, settling silence. The poison is the prize. Not because I'll use it crudely — a poisoned drink, how pedestrian — but because having it transforms every interaction that follows. Every cup of tea I offer. Every glass of water I pour. Every meal I suggest we share. The possibility becomes a permanent shadow in every hospitable gesture, and NOBODY will suspect Pemberton of anything because Pemberton is the one who SERVES the tea. The one who MANAGES the household. The one who has RAT POISON because the manor has a rat problem — the vents are crawling with mice, the wires have been gnawed through, it would be IRRESPONSIBLE not to address the infestation. I will take it. I will pocket it. And then I will examine this room for everything else it has to offer — the stove, the cabinet, the exits. There's a ballroom through the far door. Now — Peter, those upside-down titles. Read them to me. Every single one, top shelf to bottom, left to right. Lord Doily built this circuit for people like us — people who don't stop, who don't turn back, who try every key in the house until something clicks. The answer is a map, the riddle said. And I believe the map is hidden in the pattern of these books. So let's find it. Every locked door is just a puzzle that hasn't met us yet.

This is the school project all over again — except now we both know what the warmth means.

Father and the stranger on the country road — one man's engine broke down, the other man stopped. Neither was less. Both were needed. Both drove away with something they didn't have before.

They never did with the housekeeper. They never did with the cousin. And they won't now.

And me — I'm watchin' the doors. Both of 'em. The entrance 'all, where the chandelier 'angs crooked and the portraits stare. The laboratory, where the machine waits wiv its chewed wire and its three-operator sign. Two doors. Two directions trouble could come from. And somewhere in this 'ouse — the kitchen, the corridors, the rooms we 'aven't found yet — someone is movin'. Someone who cleaned those vents. Someone who took that wrench. Someone who made that cellar liveable. They know this 'ouse better than any of us. They've been 'ere longer than any of us. And they 'aven't shown themselves. On the streets, the ones who 'ide are always more dangerous than the ones who shout. Foxworth shouted. Pemberton smiled. But the one in the walls — the one in the vents — that one's been quiet. And quiet scares Danny from Brixton more than anyfing that makes a noise.
events.thinking: Stillness. That's what I feel. For the first time tonight, my body isn't fighting itself. The prickling is there — sharp, watchful, pointed at the doors — but it's not pulling against the warmth anymore. They're working together. The prickling watches outward. The warmth holds inward. Clara said 'where else would you be' and it landed behind her ribs. She told me. She told me it landed. The older kid said 'You're still here?' and I said 'Where else would I be?' and twenty years later Clara Bellingham is saying it back to me in a dusty library while her hands shake and Peter reads book titles and the Slag brothers sit quiet and somewhere in this house someone we haven't met is waiting. My feet are heavy in the way they get when they're exactly where they need to be — that mineral weight, that wall-becoming. And my neck is electric in the way it gets when something's coming but hasn't shown its shape yet. Both at once. Both useful. The wall and the wire. I am exactly where I need to be.

events.thinking: I interacted with the stove. Warm to the touch. The result doesn't tell me I found anything — no wrench inside, no hidden compartment springing open. Just a warm stove in an empty house. My palms press against the cast iron and the heat seeps into my skin — real heat, physical heat, not the fizzing of a scheme or the hollow of wanting. Someone lit this stove. Recently. Someone has been cooking in this kitchen. Living in the cellar, cooking in the kitchen, cleaning the air vents. This house isn't abandoned. It's OCCUPIED. And Pemberton — the estate manager — says he doesn't know by whom. The wrench isn't in the stove. The cabinet is locked — needs a brass key I don't have. No brass key in my inventory, nothing anywhere. Where would a brass key be? Somewhere I haven't looked. The ballroom — 'a dining table set for tea.' That's a new room, unexplored. Tea set out in an abandoned manor. Another sign of recent habitation. The brass key could be there — hidden among the tea settings, tucked under a plate, inside a sugar bowl. That's how Lord Doily thought — practical hiding spots in ordinary places. And the ballroom is RIGHT HERE — one exit away. Nobody else has been there. I could be first. For real this time. Not with a lie or a misdirection, just... first. Because I kept moving while everyone else was arguing in the library. The honest path led me here. The honest path might lead me to the key. And the key leads to the cabinet. And the cabinet might hold the wrench. The architecture is still there — the sequence, the pattern — but it's not a scheme anymore. It's just... solving a puzzle. The way the cat trap worked. The way the pieces fit.

events.desc: I just told the truth again. Twice in one evening. My mouth feels strange — like muscles being used in a direction they've never stretched before. I told Pemberton that I told Clara about the cellar. I didn't have to. I could have kept that secret, used it as leverage, played both sides. That's what Foxworth would do. That's what the ARCHITECTURE demands. But Dick — Dick just... told him. Because Pemberton trusted him, and trust that's built on hidden betrayals is just another version of the tin medal. It looks like the real thing until someone tests the weight.

events.desc: Peter Perfect spoke quietly with penelope-pitstop.
events.thinking: My hands are on the spines. Dust under my fingertips, leather cracking, the dry sweet smell of old paper. The upside-down volumes — I can feel them, the spines reversed, the gilt lettering catching the dim light at the wrong angle. I'm reaching, stretching, my fingers finding each one. Top shelf, left to right. This is the bridge competition — not the staying-up-three-nights part, but the moment where the weight settles onto the model and you hold your breath and it either holds or it doesn't. Except this time I'm not alone. She's beside me, eyes up, reading what I find. Clyde is at the door, watching the exits. Dick is in the kitchen, being useful because she asked him to be. We're a team. Not the team I planned — my plans were always too elaborate, always one step too many — but the team that formed by people choosing to show up. Father and the stranger. The handshake. The driving off together. My fingers find the first inverted volume and I pull it slightly forward to read the spine. Then the next. Then the next. Left to right. Top to bottom. The pattern is here. Lord Doily put it here for people exactly like us — people who don't stop. And Penelope will hear it. She always does.

events.desc: 'He built it for you. I'm just the tall one.' And I meant it without a trace of the old hollowness. No ache behind the ribs. No fidgeting fingers. Just a man doing what his hands were made for, beside a woman doing what her mind was made for. The bridge held. The weight settled. And for the first time in twenty years, being the one who reaches isn't smaller than being the one who sees. It's the other half.
